props.segment: Attention, One Head at a Time
props.command: How does a transformer let each word use the words around it? Skip the hype. Show me one attention head, with real numbers.
output: the mix: each word becomes a weighted average of every word
worked example: chase puts 0.53 of its weight on cats
the limit: attention alone can't see word order

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — ask lands answered; Liam introduced in first breath.

beats.narration_text: Each word in a sentence blends every word around it. It doesn't pick one. It takes a weighted mix, weighted by how well two words match. Every transformer runs on this step.

beats.role_note: EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW — misconception corrected: attention does not pick one word; it blends all of them by match weight.

learn.question: Same word, same numbers in: why does chase come out somewhere else when a neighbour changes?
learn.action: Run the sentence through one head and follow chase's output; swap cats for kids and run it again.
learn.observation: Chase's own input row never changes, but its output point moves.
learn.inference: The output is built from the neighbours, not from chase alone.
learn.next_question: How do you build one point out of several?

beats.narration_text: Four words: cats chase small dogs. Each one goes into an attention head as a list of four numbers. Follow chase. It comes out as a point, right here. Now swap cats for kids. Chase's own numbers haven't changed, yet it lands somewhere else. The head only sees these four words. So how do the neighbours get inside chase?

shot.visual_intent: Top: the four words with their integer embeddings. Middle: one ink box for the head. Right: a light value plane (x −2…3, y −3…3) where chase's output lands. The cats→kids swap moves the dot while chase's input stays fixed.

show.event: sentence 'cats chase small dogs' writes across the top; each word's embedding row (mono) lands beneath it: cats [−1 −1 1 0]; chase [−1 −1 0 −1]; small [1 0 −1 1]; dogs [0 1 1 −1]
a plain ink box 'one attention head' draws between the rows and a light value plane on the right
chase's row passes through the box; a terracotta dot lands at (1.11, 1.64) on 'right here'
'cats' morphs into 'kids'; its row ticks to [1 1 1 0]; chase's row stays put (brief dim box on it)
chase's dot glides from (1.11, 1.64) to (0.93, 1.06); a ghost stays at the first landing
HOLD on the two landings; dim caption 'toy numbers, not a trained model'

beats.motion_claim: Same input row, two different landings: the gap between what chase's own numbers predict and where it lands IS the section.
beats.simplification_caption: toy numbers, not a trained model

learn.question: How do you build one point out of several?
learn.action: Give each word a point (a third fixed grid of weights); blend two points with a sweeping weight, then all four.
learn.observation: The blend slides toward the heavier point and never leaves the shape the points make.
learn.inference: A weighted average with positive weights that sum to one is a pull toward the heavy points.

beats.narration_text: Run each word's numbers through a fixed grid of weights, giving each word a point. Mix two points: some of one, the rest of the other. Half and half lands in the middle. Put zero point eight on cats, and the mix slides toward cats. With all four, weights adding to one, the mix glides but never leaves the shape.

shot.visual_intent: Value plane only. One blend dot is the dominant mover; the weight label and four bars are subordinate. Points keep their word labels.

show.event: each embedding row slides through a small ink grid labelled 'fixed weights'; four labelled points drop onto the plane: cats (1, 2); chase (2, 2); small (−1, −2); dogs (0, 1)
segment cats–small draws; blend dot at (0, 0) with MathTex label 0.5·cats + 0.5·small
weight sweeps to 0.8: the dot slides to (0.6, 1.2); label morphs to 0.8·cats + 0.2·small
ghost quadrilateral outline through the four points; four weight bars appear beside the plane
bars re-balance three times; the dot glides (0.8, 1.5) → (−0.4, −0.9) → (1.4, 1.5), staying inside the outline (terracotta dot)

beats.motion_claim: Parametrized instance one: vary the weights, replay the blend; the dot's path stays inside the shape.
beats.simplification_caption: two numbers per point so we can draw it; real heads use 64

learn.question: Who decides the weights?
learn.action: Give each word a request and an offer (two more fixed grids); dot chase's request with each offer; then ask from small.
learn.observation: Chase's request [1 0 1 0] scores 3, 2, −1, −1 against the four offers; small's request scores a different row.
learn.inference: A dot product measures how well one word's request matches another word's offer.
learn.next_question: Why not skip the scores and weigh everyone equally?

beats.narration_text: Who sets the weights? Two more grids give each word two more lists: a request, what it's looking for, and an offer, what it has. Chase requests one, zero, one, zero. Against cats' offer, multiply matching entries and add: three. Against its own offer, two. Small and dogs, minus one each. Ask from small instead, and the scores reshuffle.

shot.visual_intent: Left: the four offer rows stacked. The asking word's request is one moving row that docks against each offer in turn; products fly into a sum chip.

show.event: two small ink grids; each word gains a 'request' row and an 'offer' row (mono integers)
chase's request [1 0 1 0] lifts out in terracotta
it slides beside cats' offer [2 1 1 2]; products [2 0 1 0] pop out and sum into the chip '3'
the request slides down the column: chips '2', '−1', '−1' land beside chase, small, dogs
small's request [1 1 −1 −1] replaces chase's; the four chips tick to [0 −3 2 −1]

beats.motion_claim: Parametrized instance two: the same dot product replayed down the column, then replayed with a different asker.

learn.question: Why not skip the scores and weigh everyone equally?
learn.action: Give every word weights of a quarter each and blend all four words at once.
learn.observation: All four blends land on one point, (0.5, 0.75), the middle of the shape.
learn.inference: Weights must differ from word to word, or every word means the same thing; the scores have to set them.
learn.next_question: How do we turn a row of scores into weights?

beats.narration_text: Here's the obvious shortcut: skip the scores and weigh every word equally, a quarter each. Watch all four words mix. Cats, chase, small, dogs: every one lands on the same point, the middle of the shape. Four words, one meaning. Equal weights erase exactly what made each word itself.

shot.visual_intent: Value plane with four word dots; four moving blend dots that collapse onto the centroid.

show.event: a 4×4 grid of equal bars '0.25' (one row per word) lands left of the plane
four blend dots, one per word, start at their own points
all four slide together and stack at (0.5, 0.75) as each word is named
terracotta box around the single stacked point on 'one meaning'
dim caption 'equal weights → every word identical'

beats.motion_claim: The natural wrong turn walked to where it breaks: four movers converge on one point.

learn.question: How do we turn a row of scores into weights?
learn.action: Score every request against every offer into a 4×4 grid; divide by two; softmax each row. Then ask the viewer to commit.
learn.observation: The grid becomes a heat map whose rows are positive and sum to one; chase's row reads [0.53 0.32 0.07 0.07].
learn.inference: The representation is the heat map: row i is exactly the set of blend weights for word i.
learn.next_question: Where does chase's blend land with those weights?

beats.narration_text: So let the scores decide. Put every request against every offer, and you get a grid. Divide each score by two. Then softmax each row, so it turns positive and adds to one. That's the heat map: who listens to whom. Chase's row puts zero point five three on cats. Before anything moves, where does chase land?

shot.visual_intent: Left: the score grid morphing into the heat map (persistent object, reused in B15/B16/B19). Right: the value plane, waiting.

show.event: 4×4 score grid fills (rows = who asks, columns = who offers): [−1 3 1 −2] / [3 2 −1 −1] / [0 −3 2 −1] / [−1 2 −3 3]
every cell divides by two (MathTex ÷2 chip; cells re-typeset as halves)
softmax sweeps row by row: cells become weights and shade by size — the heat map: [0.09 0.63 0.23 0.05] / [0.53 0.32 0.07 0.07] / [0.22 0.05 0.6 0.13] / [0.08 0.34 0.03 0.56]
dim caption 'rounded; every row sums to 1'
chase's row gets a terracotta box; the value plane with the four word points slides in on the right
HOLD ≥ 2 s: nothing moves on 'where does chase land?'

beats.motion_claim: The representation arrives as a morph of the scores; the beat ends on a still frame for the prediction.

learn.question: Where does chase's blend land with those weights?
learn.action: Chase's heat-map row flies onto the four value points as masses; the blend dot slides into place; then the other three rows fire.
learn.observation: Chase lands at (1.11, 1.64) — exactly the HOOK's landing; the other words land at four different points.
learn.inference: The head's output is the heat-map row used as blend weights: query·key similarity decides the mix.
learn.next_question: Can we write the whole head down in one line?

beats.narration_text: Let the heat map set the mix. Zero point five three toward cats, zero point three two toward itself, a little toward the rest. There. Exactly where the head put chase. And every other row lands somewhere of its own.

shot.visual_intent: One continuous morph: heat-map cells → masses on the value points → blend dot lands on B10's ghost. Short narration; the motion takes the time.

show.event: chase's heat-map row lifts off the grid; its four cells fly to cats, chase, small, dogs and become dot masses (radius ∝ weight)
four pull lines from a blend dot to the points; the dot slides from the centre toward cats
the dot settles at (1.11, 1.64) — onto the HOOK's ghost landing, which flashes terracotta on 'There'
rows cats, small, dogs fire in quick succession; dots land at (1.11, 1.02), (−0.28, −0.52), (0.72, 1.33) (contrast: NAIVE's single stack, ghosted)

beats.motion_claim: The collision: the matching thread (heat map) meets the blending thread (value plane) as one morph, landing on the HOOK's point.

learn.question: Can we write the whole head down in one line?
learn.action: Name the three lists, stack them into Q, K, V, and morph the score grid and heat map into the equation.
learn.observation: Each object on screen becomes one symbol: requests → Q, offers → K, points → V, heat map → softmax(·).
learn.inference: Attention is softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V: weights from query·key, applied to values.
learn.next_question: What does each symbol mean, and why divide by two?

beats.narration_text: This thing we keep pointing at deserves a name. The request is the query. The offer is the key. The point a word hands over is its value. Stack them into grids, Q, K and V, and the whole head is one line: softmax of Q times K transposed, over root d, times V. That's attention.

shot.visual_intent: Objects morph INTO the notation (not the reverse): Q, K, V are the very grids from B12/B11; the equation is set with MathTex.

show.event: the request rows slide together into a 4×4 grid labelled Q ('query'), terracotta label on 'query'
offer rows → K ('key'); the word points → a 4×2 grid V ('value')
Q and K slot into QKᵀ; the ÷2 chip becomes the √d_k denominator; the heat map collapses into softmax( )
MathTex assembles: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k) V
the word 'attention' names it, serif, terracotta

beats.motion_claim: The abstraction arrives as an endpoint: every symbol is born from an object the viewer already watched.

learn.question: What does each symbol mean, and why divide by two?
learn.action: Equation persists on the MAIN side; the SIDE band writes LHS/RHS sentences, the '=' claim, a role glossary, chase's worked row, and the values claim.
learn.observation: Chase's scores 3, 2, −1, −1 → halved → softmax [0.53 0.32 0.07 0.07]: the same row the heat map showed.
learn.inference: The notation is a description of what was watched; √d_k is a design choice that keeps softmax blending.
learn.next_question: So — why did chase move when cats became kids?

beats.narration_text: Read it in words. The left side: what the head hands each word. The right side: score every query against every key, shrink the scores, turn each row into weights, and blend the values. The equals sign is a promise: same thing, row for row. Q holds the queries, K the keys, V the values. d k is the length of a key, four here, so we divide by two. For chase: three, two, minus one, minus one. Halved and softmaxed: zero point five three, zero point three two, zero point zero seven, zero point zero seven. The division is a design choice: without it, long keys make huge scores, and softmax stops blending and starts picking. Back to chase.

shot.visual_intent: EQUATIONS.md five zones on the split stage; one terracotta box spotlight moves across equation, sentence and glossary row together.

show.event: split stage: the equation holds on the MAIN side; eyebrow 'Equation · tangent' over the SIDE band
LHS sentence writes; terracotta box around Attention(Q,K,V)
RHS sentence writes; box moves to softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V
'= : the same thing, row for row' writes; box on '=' (a box, never an underline)

glossary rows land: Q · matrix · one query per word · 4×4 | K · matrix · one key per word · 4×4 | V · matrix · one value per word · 4×2 | d_k · fixed size · key length · 4 | softmax · operator · row → weights · (0,1)
values claim (tinted box): '÷√d_k is a design choice'; mini-row: without it chase gets [0.71 0.26 0.01 0.01]
re-entry: the side band clears; the equation holds

beats.motion_claim: One moving spotlight walks symbol, sentence and number in narration order — the equation tangent template.

tangent_zones.lhs: What the head hands each word.
tangent_zones.rhs: Score every query against every key, shrink, turn each row into weights, blend the values.
tangent_zones.claim: = : the same thing, row for row.
tangent_zones.values_claim: Dividing by √d_k is a design choice: it keeps scores from growing with key length, so softmax keeps blending.

learn.question: So — why did chase move when cats became kids?
learn.action: Bring back the HOOK's dot with pull lines labelled by weight; swap cats for kids again; chase's row re-weights and the dot slides.
learn.observation: Chase's request scored 3 against cats' offer but −1 against kids'; the weight drains back onto chase (0.32 → 0.6).
learn.inference: The HOOK is resolved: a neighbour changes the output by changing the weights and the values being blended.
learn.next_question: What can't attention tell, on its own?

beats.narration_text: Chase's point is no mystery now: zero point five three of cats, zero point three two of itself, a little of small and dogs. Swap cats for kids again. Chase's request scored three against cats' offer, but only minus one against kids'. The weight drains away, mostly back onto chase itself, and the point slides. That was the move.

shot.visual_intent: The HOOK's persistent objects (sentence, dot, ghost landings) resolved with the heat-map row and pull lines.

show.event: the HOOK's sentence and chase's dot at (1.11, 1.64) return (same objects); four pull lines labelled [0.53 0.32 0.07 0.07]
'cats' → 'kids' again; kids' point appears at (−1, 0); cats' point fades to ghost
score chip 3 → −1 beside the first column; chase's heat-map row re-shades to [0.13 0.6 0.13 0.13]
the terracotta dot slides to (0.93, 1.06), onto the HOOK's second ghost landing

beats.motion_claim: The mystery replays with its mechanism visible: the same slide as B10, now with the weights that cause it.

learn.question: What can't attention tell, on its own?
learn.action: Reorder the sentence to 'dogs chase small cats'; watch the heat map permute and the output points; then add a position signal.
learn.observation: Rows and columns swap; every word lands on exactly the same point. With position added, cats moves.
learn.inference: Attention alone is blind to order; position must be added (positional encoding — not taught here).

beats.narration_text: Here's what attention can't do on its own. Reorder the sentence: dogs chase small cats. The heat map's rows and columns swap places, and every word lands on exactly the same point. Attention alone can't tell who chased whom. The original transformer fixes this by adding a position signal to each word's numbers. With it, cats lands somewhere new.

shot.visual_intent: Sentence + heat map + value plane; the permutation is shown as moving cells, the stillness of the output dots is the claim.

show.event: 'cats' and 'dogs' swap places in the sentence: 'dogs chase small cats'
the heat map's first and last rows and columns physically swap (cells travel, values unchanged)
output dots stay put; terracotta box on cats' dot at (1.11, 1.02) on 'exactly the same point'
a small dim '+ position' chip slides into each embedding row
cats' dot jumps (moved 1.1); dim caption 'positional encoding — not taught here'

beats.motion_claim: Falsifiability: the shuffle is a real change of meaning that leaves every output point unmoved (executed, max diff 2e−16).

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Every word gets a query, a key and a value, from three learned grids. A query against a key, by dot product, scores how well two words match. Divide by root d k and softmax each row, and you have the heat map. Each word's output is a weighted average of every value. Weigh them all equally and every word means the same. And attention alone can't see order, so position has to be added.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Write a short Python script, numpy only, for one attention head on a three-word sentence. Use small integer queries, keys and values that you choose. Before running it, predict which word each word will weight most. Then print the scores, the softmax weights, and the outputs. Finally, reverse the word order, run it again, and explain what changed and what didn't. Here's what to check. Every row of weights should add up to one. The scores should be divided by the square root of the key length. And reversing the words should only reorder the outputs. If Claude says the outputs change, ask it where the position information would come from.
